DILG BAGONG PIU-PINAS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, west Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq.gov.ph OPINION NO. S. JUL 03 2024 ATTY. LUISITO C. DEVEZA Managing Partner Padiemos & Padiernos Law Offices Dear Atty. Deveza: This has reference to the request for legal opinion regarding the power of the local government unit over national and arterial roads and its power to prohibit the passage of public transportation, specifically public utility buses. In a hypothetical scenario you mentioned, the following points of classifications were raised, to wit: (I) Does the prohibition by City X through Resolution Y of the use of a Primary National road violate the Franchise route given to public utility buses with such route as granted by the Land Transportation, Franchise and Regulatory Board (LTFRB)?; (2) Does the failure of the LGU to conduct public hearing create a substantive defect to Resolution Y as it failed to comply with the requirements?; (3) Does the failure of the LGU to include in its Resolution the intent for such Prohibition violate the reasonable standard and means test needed for the passage of an ordinance?; and (4) Does the absolute discretion given to the Mayor of City X without check and balance and to include the prohibition in the use of National Road in excess of power and thus, should be invalid under existing laws?. We resolve. On the first matter, transportation plans from LGUs, duly approved by the Sanggunians, shall be made in accordance with the policies and subsequent issuances and guidelines from the Department of Transportation (DOTr)1. We cite the pertinent provision of the Department Order (DO) 2017-011 which provides that in case of Route Modification, LGUs may propose modifications in routes for review and approval of the LTFRB and the DOTr. The proposal for route modifications should include the rationale or justification for the changes. In light of the aforementioned, we opine that a city cannot unilaterally prohibit the use of a primary national road without violating the rules and regulations of the DOTr. Anent the second matter, under the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), prior public hearings are required where: (I ) local govemment site, offices and facilities are to be transferred2; (2) reclassification of agricultural lands3, (3) contribution of funds, Sec. 3.1.6 of DO 2017-011, OMNIBUS GUIDELINES ON THE PLANNING AND IDENTIFICATION OF PUBLIC ROAD TRANSPORTATION SERVICES AND FRANCHISE ISSUANCE par (b) Sec 11 of RA 7160 Sec. 20, LGC. real estate, equipment, and other kinds of property and appointments or assignment of personnel in support of undertakings commonly beneficial to local govemment units which have grouped themselves, consolidated or coordinated their efforts, services and resources4; (4) levy of taxes, fees, charges on any base or subject not otherwise specifically enumerated in the Local Govemment Code as taxed under the NIRC, as amended, or other applicable laws5; and enactment of local tax ordinances and revenue measures67. Applying the foregoing to the instant case, the failure of the LGU to conduct public hearing did not affect the validity of the resolution it has issued. On the question of the reasonable standard and means test, the Court has consistently ruled that in order for an ordinance to be valid, it must not only be within the corporate powers of the concerned local govemment unit to enact, but must also be passed in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law. Moreover, substantively, the ordinance: (I) must not contravene the Constitution or any statute; (2) must not be unfair or oppressive; (3) must not be partial or discriminatory; (4) must not prohibit, but may regulate trade; (5) must be general and consistent with public policy; and (6) must not be unreasonable. Hence, with regard to this point of clarification, we opine that the failure to include the intent for prohibition in the Resolution will not affect its validity. Settled is the rule that every law, including ordinances, or resolutions, in this case, is presumed valid. This presumption may be set aside when invalidity or unreasonableness: (1) appears on the face of the ordinance, or (2) is established by proper evidence8. As to the last issue, we opine that official acts of the local chief executive enjoy the presumption of regularity. The same may be overcome by contrary evidence before the regular courts of justice or tribunals and administrative bodies having jurisdiction on the same. Finally, this opinion of this Department is based solely on the facts and representations narrated from the letter and our appreciation of the same. Further, this opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have assisted you on this matter. Thank you very much. Very truly yours, RITY OF THE SECRETARY: N C RR. LLAMAS e retary for External, Legal and Legislative OUS JVRULLLS-LRALLD/sbl sec. 33, LGC. Sec. 186, LGC. 6 Sec. 187. LGC.
